chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥalabī and Ibn Abī ‘Umayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, who said:

I asked Abū ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who purchased from another man with a dīnār, taking half of it as goods (bay‘) and half as slave-girls (warīq). He said, 'There is no harm in it.' And I asked him if it is permissible for him to take half as slave-girls or goods and leave the other half until later, then take it as slave-girls or goods. He said, 'I dislike that he leave anything from it until he takes all of it, so let him not do that.' (431)

37 [3-18-617-4] - As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ‘Īsā narrated, from al-Ḥasan ibn ‘Alī al-Washshā’, from Tha‘labah ibn Maymūn, from Abū al-Ḥasan (1) al-Ṣābāṭī, from ‘Ammār ibn Mūsā al-Ṣābāṭī, who said: 'I heard Abū ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) saying: There is no harm in a man selling a dīnār for more than the exchange rate of that day, deferred (nasi’ah).'

key_terms.دِينَار: Dinar, a gold coin used as currency
key_terms.نَسِيئَةً: Nasi’ah, a deferred payment or credit sale
key_terms.وَرِق: Warīq, referring to silver coins or slave-girls in this context

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell gold coins for a deferred price higher than the current market rate in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of mixed currency transactions, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) permits buying two distinct assets with one dinar but advises against deferring the acquisition of the second asset to avoid uncertainty (gharar). The second report highlights the permissibility of selling gold for a higher price on credit (nasi'ah), distinguishing it from the strict prohibition of gold-for-gold exchanges with delay, a key distinction in Shia commercial jurisprudence. These rulings reflect the Imams' practical approach to trade, balancing permissibility with the recommendation of certainty in contractual obligations.
